dublinCore.title: Pythagorean Theorem MicroSim
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Geometry
Pythagorean Theorem
Right Triangles
Area of a Square
Interactive Simulation
dublinCore.description: A p5.js MicroSim in which two sliders set the legs of a right triangle and a Show Squares button draws a square on each of the three sides, so learners can see that the areas of the two smaller squares add up to the area of the square on the hypotenuse. A readout panel lists each side length and each area.

topic: Pythagorean theorem: the squares on the two legs of a right triangle add up to the square on the hypotenuse
learningObjectives: The learner will explain why the areas of the squares on the two legs of a right triangle add up to the area of the square on the hypotenuse.
The learner will calculate the length of the hypotenuse from the lengths of the two legs.
prerequisites: The area of a square is its side length multiplied by itself
Squares and square roots of whole numbers
The parts of a right triangle: the right angle, the two legs and the hypotenuse

curriculumStandards.framework: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics
curriculumStandards.description: Explain a proof of the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse.

curriculumStandards.framework: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics
curriculumStandards.description: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to determine unknown side lengths in right triangles in real-world and mathematical problems in two and three dimensions.

misconceptions.misconception: The hypotenuse equals the sum of the legs: c = a + b.
misconceptions.correction: The areas add, not the lengths.

misconceptions.misconception: Doubling the sides doubles the areas.
misconceptions.correction: Each area becomes four times as large.

misconceptions.misconception: The theorem only works for whole-number triangles such as 3, 4, 5.
misconceptions.correction: It holds for every right triangle.

accessibility.screenReaderScript: A right triangle with a horizontal side a, a vertical side b and a hypotenuse c. Two sliders set the lengths of side a and side b from 50 to 130. A Show Squares button draws a green square on side a, a blue square on side b and a pink square on side c. A readout panel lists the length of each side and the area of each square, and shows that the area of square a plus the area of square b always equals the area of square c. A Reset button returns both sides to 100.

userInterface.layoutPattern: Figure beside the title and readout panel at 500 pixels and wider; title and readout panel above the figure on a narrower canvas. Two parameter sliders and a reveal button with a linked readout panel

responsiveBreakpoints.description: At this width and wider, the figure sits beside the title and the readout panel. On a narrower canvas, the title and the readout panel sit above the figure

controls.label: Show Squares / Hide Squares
controls.description: Show or hide the square on each side of the triangle (progressive disclosure). The squares start hidden

controls.label: Reset
controls.description: Return side a and side b to 100. The squares stay shown or hidden

visualElements.description: A square on each side of the triangle: green on side a, blue on side b and pink on side c. Every colored square is also named by a text label

assumptions: The angle between side a and side b is always 90 degrees
limitations: Side a and side b are whole numbers from 50 to 130
Side c is rounded to two decimal places, so squaring the displayed value of c can differ slightly from the displayed c²
The MicroSim shows that the areas agree. It does not show a proof of why they agree

variables.name: side a
variables.description: Leg: the horizontal side of the triangle

variables.name: side b
variables.description: Leg: the vertical side of the triangle

instructionalStrategies: Predict-test-explain with progressive disclosure: explore the triangle first, then reveal the squares
Immediate feedback: the readout panel updates as each slider moves

assessmentQuestions.question: When side a grows by 30, why does side c grow by less than 30?
What is the same about the three areas at every slider setting?
Which slider settings make side c a whole number?
When both legs double, what happens to side c and to the three areas?
Predict how side c changes when one leg changes.
Make a table of a², b² and c² for three slider settings, and state the pattern in words.
Calculate the hypotenuse for a new pair of legs, then check it with the MicroSim.
